stem: A 32-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department due to fever, night sweats, and chills over the last several days.  The patient reports recent intravenous drug use.  He has otherwise been in good health with no other medical problems.  Temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F), blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg, and pulse is 105/min and regular.  Further evaluation reveals aortic valve endocarditis with an intracardiac abscess and formation of a small fistula between the right ventricle and aortic root that remains patent throughout the cardiac cycle.  Doppler ultrasonographic examination of the fistula will most likely reveal which of the following blood flow patterns?​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​

options.label: A
options.text: Flow from the aortic root to the right ventricle continuously

options.label: B
options.text: Flow from the aortic root to the right ventricle only in diastole

options.label: C
options.text: Flow from the aortic root to the right ventricle only in systole

options.label: D
options.text: Flow from the right ventricle to the aortic root continuously

options.label: E
options.text: Flow from the right ventricle to the aortic root only in diastole

options.label: F
options.text: Flow from the right ventricle to the aortic root only in systole

explanation:
This patient with aortic valve endocarditis has developed an intracardiac fistula between the aortic root and the right ventricle.  Aortocavitary fistulas are an uncommon complication of bacterial endocarditis caused by extension of the infection from the valve into the adjacent myocardium.

Echocardiography with Doppler analysis can be used to detect and quantify shunts in patients with intracardiac fistulas.  Because aortic pressure (eg, 120/80 mm Hg) exceeds right ventricular pressure (eg, 25/2 mm Hg) throughout the cardiac cycle (ie, during both systole and diastole), this patient's shunt is expected to demonstrate continuous blood flow from the higher-pressure aortic root to the lower-pressure right ventricle.  This continuous flow pattern typically causes a continuous murmur on cardiac auscultation.

A similar flow pattern causing a continuous bruit is expected with most arteriovenous fistulas (eg, femoral artery to femoral vein) because systemic arterial pressure substantially exceeds systemic venous pressure throughout the cardiac cycle.

(Choice B)  Because aortic pressure exceeds right ventricular pressure throughout the cardiac cycle (both systole and diastole), flow through this patient's fistula is expected to be continuous and not isolated to diastole.

(Choice C)  A ventricular septal defect typically causes shunting mostly during systole.  This is because left ventricular pressure is greater than right ventricular pressure during systole, but the pressures are relatively similar during diastole (ie, minimal flow takes place during diastole).

(Choices D, E, and F)  Pressure in the aortic root is greater than in the right ventricle throughout the cardiac cycle (both systole and diastole); therefore, blood flow from the right ventricle to the aortic root would not be expected in this patient.

Educational objective:Aortic pressure is higher than right ventricular pressure throughout the cardiac cycle (ie, during both systole and diastole).  Consequently, an intracardiac fistula between the aortic root and the right ventricle demonstrates continuous blood flow from the aortic root (high pressure) to the right ventricle (low pressure).​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​
